pages.title: Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
pages.text:
Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration 
 Calibration: Speaker and Headphone Level Calibration
 When you set up and calibrate speakers, there are three things to worry about: loudness, frequency response, and phase. This page covers loudness only. Once your monitoring system is calibrated for loudness, every mixing decision you make is based on a level you can trust and repeat.
 Why Loudness Calibration Matters
 If you monitor too loud, your mix will end up too quiet.
 If you monitor too quiet, your mix will end up too loud.
 If you do not pay attention to your monitoring level at all, you will deliver inconsistent mixes to your clients.
 The Six Gain Stages
 Loudness is controlled at six possible points between your DAW and your ears. Two of these stages change the actual audio in your final mix file. The other four only change how loud that file sounds to you in the room, without touching the file itself.
 Channel Fader
 The volume fader on an individual channel of a DAW. It controls the volume of a single instrument or vocal performance inside the mix.
 Affects the final mix: changing this fader changes the sound of your bounced mix file. 
 Master Fader
 The volume control for the master bus of a DAW. It is the final gain stage before the mix file is created and, on most sessions, is the last thing you would ever touch. It almost never moves except to automate a fade-out.
 Affects the final mix: changing this fader changes the sound of your bounced mix file. 
 Computer Volume
 The volume fader of the computer you are working on. If you are listening on headphones plugged directly into the computer, this is likely the last gain stage before your ears.
 Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself. 
 Interface
 The output volume control on the interface you are using. This is sometimes a knob on the front of the interface, and it is sometimes controlled digitally through software. It functions like a small monitor section, similar to what you would find on an analog console.
 Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself. 
 Monitor Controller
 A device used to control the volume of studio monitors, often across multiple monitor sets at the press of a button. Some units control stereo pairs only. Others handle 5.1, 7.1, or full Dolby Atmos systems, and a well-equipped monitor controller can manage volume, signal processing, phase, and delay across more than 64 separate monitor signals at once.
 Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself. 
 Amplifier Volume
 The volume control on the amplifiers connected directly to your speakers. Active (powered) speakers have the amplifier built in. Passive (unpowered) speakers receive power from a separate amplifier. Every speaker that carries a discrete signal should have its own power amplifier.
 Does not affect the final mix: it changes your perception of the mix, not the mix file itself. 
 Volume Controllers at a Glance
 The six gain stages and whether each one changes the final mix file
 Stage
 What It Is
 Affects Final Mix File?
 Channel Fader
 Volume fader on an individual channel of a DAW
 Yes
 Master Fader
 Volume control for the master bus of a DAW
 Yes
 Computer Volume
 Volume fader of the computer you are working on
 No
 Interface
 Output volume control on the interface you are using
 No
 Monitor Controller
 Device used to control the volume of studio monitors
 No
 Amplifier Volume
 Volume control of the amplifiers connected directly to the speakers
 No
 Which Controller Should You Use for Overall Volume?
 Recommendation for each gain stage when setting your main listening level
 Stage
 Use It for Overall Volume?
 Why
 Channel Fader
 No
 It controls one channel, not the whole mix.
 Master Fader
 No
 Using it as a volume control changes your final mix file, sometimes for the worse.
 Computer Volume
 Possibly
 Use it if your speakers connect directly to the computer or you only have headphones and no interface.
 Interface
 Possibly
 Use it if you do not have a monitor controller.
 Monitor Controller
 Yes
 Adjusting overall volume is exactly what this device is for. Use it if you have one.
 Amplifier Volume
 No
 Changing amplifier volume forces you to re-calibrate every time.
 Calibrating Your Speakers
 Once you know which controller you are using for overall volume, follow these steps.
 Decide how you want to control your overall speaker volume.
 Send a test signal through the system.
 Measure the signal coming out of the speakers with an SPL meter, or your ears once you are experienced enough.
 Adjust the power amplifiers of your speakers so each speaker sits at the same volume and at a good level.
 Mark or note where your overall speaker volume controller is set so you can return to that position.
 Do not touch any other gain stage again, unless you are calibrating it again.
 Choosing a Test Signal
 Send one of the following through your system to calibrate against.
 Music
 Choose a song that is well mixed and holds a consistent level throughout. Frequency content and overall loudness vary greatly between songs, which makes music the least reliable of the three test signals.
 Pink Noise (-20 dB)
 Noise with equal energy per octave. It is a full-range signal that works well for measuring average loudness.
 M Noise (-20 dB)
 Developed by Meyer Sound, M Noise carries more of the qualities of real music than pink noise does. Learn more at m-noise.org (opens in a new tab).
 Measuring the Signal
 Use an SPL meter when you can get one. Phone-based SPL metering apps work as a backup, though results vary between apps and devices.
 Here is the math behind the target level: if you want 20 dB of headroom, your test signal averages -20 dBFS, and your speakers are rated for 105 dB SPL or higher, aim for 85 dB SPL on your meter at the mix position.
 Test one speaker at a time. Confirm both speakers measure exactly the same before moving on. 
 Level Reference Chart
 How different metering scales relate to each other
 Reference Point
 dB SPL
 dB FS
 dB VU
 dBu
 dBV
 Where clipping begins
 105 dB SPL
 0 dB FS
 +20 dB VU
 +24 dBu
 +21.78 dBV
 Equivalent to 0 dB VU, 20 dB headroom
 85 dB SPL
 -20 dB FS
 0 dB VU
 Pro line level +4 dBu
 +1.78 dBV
 Equivalent to consumer line level
 N/A
 N/A
 N/A
 -7.78 dBu
 Consumer line level -10 dBV
 Additional levels of note
 N/A
 N/A
 N/A
 Mic level -60 to -45 dBu
 N/A
 Threshold of human hearing
 0 dB SPL
 N/A
 N/A
 N/A
 N/A
 Adjusting the Power Amplifiers
 If your signal reads too soft or too loud, adjust the power amplifiers until each speaker matches the target level of 85 dB SPL. Send signal to one speaker at a time, and confirm both speakers measure exactly the same before you finish.
 Marking Your Calibrated Position
 Mark or note where your chosen main volume controller sits at your calibrated level, so you can return to that exact position every time.
 Not every monitor controller reads actual SPL. Some let you set the dial to show the real SPL at the mix position, so a dial reading of 85 dB truly means 85 dB in the room. Many are not that precise. Either way, mark or note where 85 dB SPL falls on your dial. 
 Do Not Touch Any Other Gain Stage Again
 Changing the amplifier volume breaks your calibration. Use only the controller you designated as the main controller to adjust volume. Use your 85 dB mark as an anchor so you always know where you stand. 
 Mixing at 85 dB is too loud for many projects, and that is fine. To find a comfortable working level, choose a piece of music that matches the style and loudness you are aiming for and play it through your system. Turn the main level down until it feels comfortable, then mark that new position so you know exactly what to return to.
 Establishing a Headphone Reference Listening Level
 You cannot hold a standard SPL meter up to a headphone driver and get a meaningful loudspeaker-style measurement. The pressure at your eardrum depends on the enclosed ear volume, pad seal, headphone placement, your pinna, and your ear canal, none of which a handheld meter accounts for. Genuine standardized headphone measurement requires an acoustic coupler, ear simulator, or HATS (head and torso simulator) system under IEC 60268-7.
 A handheld SPL meter is not a valid way to calibrate headphones to an absolute SPL. 
 Three ways to set a headphone listening level, from least to most rigorous
 Method
 What It Establishes
 Good For
 Comfortable personal level
 A subjective, non-repeatable listening level
 A quick mixing anchor when no other method is available
 Loudness matching to calibrated monitors
 A repeatable perceptual reference
 The standard classroom method used in this course
 Ear simulator / HATS measurement
 Actual standardized acoustic SPL at the eardrum
 Lab, research, and manufacturer testing
 Loudness-Matching Method
 This course uses the loudness-matching approach described in ITU-R BS.1116: calibrate your monitors first, then match the headphones to that calibrated sound field by ear.
 Set the DAW master output to unity gain.
 Load a standardized pink noise calibration signal at a known digital level.
 Calibrate your loudspeaker reference level with an SPL meter, following the speaker calibration steps above.
 Sit in the calibrated listening position and listen to the pink noise through the monitors.
 Switch to the headphones without changing the digital signal level.
 Adjust only the headphone amplifier or headphone output level until the headphones sound approximately equal in loudness to the calibrated monitors.
 Switch between the monitors and the headphones several times to refine the match.
 Mark or record the headphone level setting. This is your headphone reference listening level.
 Return to this reference level regularly while working, even though you will monitor quieter or louder at times. Spend most of your working time at moderate levels and keep louder checks brief.
 The reference chain, in order: -18 dBFS pink noise, calibrated monitors at 78 dBA, headphones matched by ear to the monitors, then the headphone level marked as your reference. 
 There is no universal 85 dB SPL headphone standard equivalent to loudspeaker calibration practice. The 78 dBA figure above comes from the loudspeaker reference level in ITU-R BS.1116 and EBU Tech 3276, not from a headphone-specific target. The lesson here is the distinction between digital reference level, acoustic reference level, monitor calibration, and subjective loudness, not a single magic number.
 Do not confuse this with hearing-safety guidance. ITU-T H.870 recommends 80 dBA for up to 40 hours a week as a safe listening exposure limit. That is a hearing-safety recommendation, not a mixing calibration target. 
 Ear Simulator / HATS Measurement
 Actual measured headphone SPL requires calibrated hardware. This is beyond the equipment used in this course, but you should know the procedure exists: calibrate a measurement microphone or ear simulator appropriate to the headphone type, seat the headphone on the fixture per the measurement procedure, play a defined calibration signal at a defined digital level, measure each channel separately, adjust the headphone amplifier to the target acoustic output, and reseat the headphones several times since pad position and seal materially affect the reading. Record the headphone model, interface, amplifier setting, test signal level, measurement weighting, fixture, and measured SPL. IEC 60268-7 is the current standard for headphone and earphone measurement, and the IEC 60318 family defines the ear and head simulators used to perform it.
 Figure 1. A broken seal loses the low end first. Glasses, long hair and a worn earpad all cost you bass you will then try to fix in the mix.
 Figure 2. How headphone response is actually measured. The microphone sits where your eardrum would be, which is why published curves differ between labs.

pages.title: Calibration: Reference Noise Files
pages.text:
Calibration: Reference Noise Files 
 Calibration: Reference Noise Files
 Figure 1. Headphone Seal Cross Section.
 Two calibration files are provided below for use in the Core Mixing studio: a pink noise reference and an M Noise reference. Both are used to check that your monitoring level is set correctly before you start a mix, but they are not interchangeable, and understanding why matters for anyone doing critical listening work.
 Download the calibration files: 
 Calibration-PinkNoise-48kHz-24bit.wav (24-bit / 48kHz, ~31 seconds)
 Calibration-MNoise-96kHz-16bit.wav (16-bit / 96kHz, ~53 seconds)
 Why We Do Not Use White Noise
 White noise carries equal energy at every frequency on a linear scale. That sounds like a fair, neutral test signal, but human hearing and most acoustic measurement do not work on a linear frequency scale, they work in octaves. Each time you go up an octave, the number of frequencies packed into that octave doubles. Since white noise has equal energy per frequency, an octave with twice as many frequencies in it ends up with twice as much total energy. The practical result is that white noise sounds like it is getting louder and brighter as you go up in pitch, roughly 3 dB per octave. That tilt makes it a poor reference for anything involving level matching, speaker calibration, or perceived tonal balance, because the signal itself is not tonally neutral to begin with.
 Pink Noise
 Pink noise corrects for the octave problem by shaping the spectrum so that energy is equal per octave rather than equal per frequency. That means the low octaves and the high octaves each carry the same total power, which matches how we perceive loudness across the frequency range far better than white noise does. This is why pink noise became the long-standing standard for setting monitor levels, checking speaker balance left to right, and doing basic room response checks with an SPL meter. It sounds noticeably darker than white noise, closer to a steady rushing or hissing sound with the harshness rolled off the top end.
 Pink noise still has a limitation for modern calibration work. Real program material, especially music and dialogue, is not a smooth, static full-spectrum signal the way pink noise is. Pink noise can make a room or a set of speakers look calibrated on paper while still leaving level-matching judgments during actual mixing sessions feeling inconsistent.
 M Noise
 M Noise is a newer calibration signal developed specifically to address that gap. Instead of a smooth, unchanging spectrum, M Noise is built from real musical program material that has been processed to retain the statistical loudness and crest-factor characteristics of actual music while remaining repeatable and measurable like a test tone. It was developed through research aimed at large-format sound reinforcement and cinema calibration, and it has increasingly replaced pink noise as the reference signal of choice for loudspeaker and room calibration where the goal is matching what a system will actually sound like under real program material, not just a synthetic average.
 Tip: 
 If you see a plugin or a piece of gear referencing "M Noise" and are not sure what it means, it is not a typo for "pink noise." It is a distinct, purpose-built signal with a different statistical structure.
 Other Noise Colors You Might Encounter
 Pink and white are the two you will use most often in this program, but the "noise color" naming system extends further, borrowed from the same visible-light spectrum analogy that gives pink noise its name.
 Brown noise (also called red noise) - falls off at 6 dB per octave, twice as steep as pink noise. It sounds deep and rumbling, closer to a low waterfall or distant thunder. The name references Brownian motion, the random-walk process it is mathematically derived from, rather than the color brown itself. Occasionally used for testing subwoofer and low-frequency extension. 
 Blue noise - the inverse of pink noise, rising at 3 dB per octave. It sounds thin and hissy, weighted heavily toward the high end. Used in some dithering algorithms because ear sensitivity to that kind of high-frequency noise shaping is comparatively low. 
 Violet noise (also called purple noise) - rises at 6 dB per octave, the mirror image of brown noise. Extremely bright and harsh. Sometimes used to test tweeter response or to analyze quantization noise, since quantization error itself tends to have a violet-like spectrum. 
 Gray noise - white noise that has been reshaped using an equal-loudness contour, so that it is perceptually flat to human hearing rather than mathematically flat across frequency. It sounds smoother and less harsh than white noise for the same reason pink noise does, but the correction curve is based on psychoacoustic loudness perception rather than the octave-energy math pink noise uses. 
 Other Common Test Signals
 A few additional signals show up often enough in calibration and testing work that they are worth knowing by name, even though they are not part of the noise-color family.
 Pure tones (sine sweeps) - a single frequency, or a sweep through a range of frequencies, used to measure the response of a specific speaker, room mode, or piece of gear at precise points rather than across the whole spectrum at once. 
 Reference tones (1 kHz, -18 dBFS or -20 dBFS) - a steady single-frequency tone at a defined digital level, used to align meter calibration between different pieces of gear or different rooms, rather than to test frequency response. 
 Note: 
 This page is reference material only. It is not an assignment and nothing here needs to be submitted.

pages.title: Calibration and Monitoring: MS (Mid-Side) Matrix
pages.text:
Calibration and Monitoring: MS (Mid-Side) Matrix 
 Calibration and Monitoring: MS (Mid-Side) Matrix
 Figure 1. Mid is the sum, side is the difference. Everything a mid-side matrix does follows from those two operations.
 This page explains the Mid-Side (MS) microphone technique and how to set up the decoding matrix required in Pro Tools Lab 02. Read through this before you start the timer.
 What Is the Mid-Side Technique?
 Mid-Side is a coincident stereo microphone technique that records two separate signals:
 Mid (M): A cardioid or omnidirectional microphone pointing directly at the source. This captures the center image. 
 Side (S): A figure-8 (bidirectional) microphone positioned at 90 degrees to the Mid mic, with its positive lobe facing left. This captures the difference between left and right. 
 Why bother? MS gives you mono-compatible recordings and lets you adjust the stereo width after recording by changing the level of the Side signal. It is widely used in classical, broadcast, and location recording. 
 The file 02_Pair_FrontMS in your session is a two-channel interleaved stereo file where the Left channel = Mid and the Right channel = Side. These are raw signals. They cannot be listened to directly as a stereo pair without decoding them first.
 The Decoding Formula
 To convert MS into a normal Left/Right stereo pair, you use this matrix:
 MS Decoding Matrix
 Output Channel
 Formula
 What You Hear
 Left
 Mid + Side
 Center plus left-leaning ambience
 Center (sum)
 Mid only
 Pure center image (mono compatible)
 Right
 Mid - Side
 Center plus right-leaning ambience (Side inverted)
 Where the x 0.5 in the diagram went. The signal flow figure shows a 0.5 gain stage on each decoded output, because M + S is twice the original Left and the matrix would come back 6 dB hot without it. In the three track build below that job belongs to the Side track faders, which is also how you set the width: pull both Side tracks down together for a narrower image, push them up for a wider one. Keep them matched, or the image pulls to one side.
 The key insight: to create the Right channel, you need a copy of the Side signal with its polarity flipped (inverted). This is why you need to use the EQ 3 polarity invert on one of the Side copies.
 Step 1: Identify the Side Mic in Your Import
 When you import the MS file, Pro Tools may create a stereo track with both channels grouped together. Before you can build the matrix, you need to identify which channel is the ambient (Side) mic and which is the Mid. For this assignment the convention is:
 Left channel = Mid mic (cardioid, pointing at the source) 
 Right channel = Side mic (figure-8, the ambient mic capturing the stereo difference signal) 
 Solo the stereo track and listen to each channel individually using the channel solo buttons in the Mix window to confirm which is which before you split. The Side mic will sound diffuse and ambient with an unusual phase character, it is not meant to be listened to alone.
 Step 2: Split the Stereo Track into Two Mono Tracks
 A stereo track in Pro Tools keeps both channels locked together. To work with Mid and Side independently you need to break the track into separate mono tracks.
 Select the stereo track in the Edit window. 
 Go to Track > Split Into Mono. Pro Tools creates two new mono tracks, one for the left channel and one for the right channel. 
 The original stereo track remains. Mute it or delete it, you will work exclusively from the two new mono tracks. 
 Rename the two new tracks immediately. If they came in with generic names, rename them now: the left-channel track is your Mid track, the right-channel track is your Side track. Clear naming here prevents confusion in every step that follows. 
 Note: After a Split Into Mono, Pro Tools appends .L and .R to the original track name. Rename both tracks before continuing. Generic names like 02_Pair_FrontMS.L will cause confusion when you duplicate the Side track in the next step.
 Step 3: Duplicate the Side Track
 The matrix requires two copies of the Side signal: one for the Left decode and one for the Right decode (polarity inverted). Duplicate the Side track to create the second copy.
 Select your Side track in the Edit window. 
 Press Option + Shift + D (Mac) to open the Duplicate Track dialog. 
 In the dialog, make sure Playlist is checked (it is the first option). This carries the audio regions across to the duplicate. Leave Insert After Last Selected Track checked so it lands in a logical position. 
 Click OK. You now have two Side tracks. Rename them clearly: one will become MS L (Side normal) and the other will become MS R (Side inverted). 
 Tip: If Playlist is not checked in the Duplicate Track dialog, the new track will be empty. It creates the track structure but does not copy the audio regions. Always verify Playlist is checked before clicking OK.
 Step 4: Build the Three Matrix Tracks
 You should now have three mono tracks. Rename and configure each one as follows:
 02 - MS L: The Side track (normal polarity). Pan hard left. This track carries the Side signal only. Panned hard left it sums with the centred Mid track, and that sum is Mid + Side at the left output. No polarity invert. 
 03 - MS C: The Mid track. Pan center. This track carries only the Mid signal = Center output. No polarity invert. 
 04 - MS R: The duplicate Side track. Pan hard right. Insert EQ 3 1-Band and activate the polarity invert button. This track carries the inverted Side signal only. Panned hard right it sums with the centred Mid track, and that sum is Mid minus Side at the right output. 
 Note: Polarity invert is not the same as phase shift. Polarity invert flips the entire waveform 180 degrees at all frequencies simultaneously. This is what MS decoding requires. A phase shift plug-in would be incorrect here.
 Step 5: Mix Group the Side Tracks
 Tracks MS L and MS R are both derived from the Side mic. They should always move together in level so the stereo decode stays balanced. Create a Mix Group for just these two tracks so their faders move together.
 Select tracks MS L and MS R in the Mix or Edit window (Command-click to select both). 
 Press Command + G to open the Create Group dialog. 
 Set the Group Type to Mix (not Edit, and not Mix/Edit, you only need fader control here). Name the group MS Sides or similar. 
 Make sure Main Volume is checked under the attributes. Click OK. 
 With this group active, raising or lowering either Side track fader moves both simultaneously. This lets you adjust the width of the MS decode (more Side = wider, less Side = narrower) without unbalancing left and right.
 Step 6: Place the Three Tracks in a Routing Folder
 Put the three MS tracks (MS L, MS C, MS R) into a routing folder to keep the session organized and to provide a single bus for feeding the rest of the mix.
 Select all three MS tracks. 
 Go to Track > Create Folder Track (or drag the tracks into an existing folder). Name the folder MS. 
 A routing folder routes the output of all tracks inside it through a single bus. This gives you a master fader for the entire MS group, useful for riding the overall level of the pair against the rest of the session. 
 Why Three Tracks Instead of Two?
 Standard MS decode produces a Left and Right stereo pair, two outputs. This assignment asks for three tracks (MS L, MS C, MS R) because it gives you independent control over each decoded element:
 MS L panned hard left, carries the Left decode 
 MS C panned center, carries only the Mid signal, reinforcing the center image 
 MS R panned hard right, carries the Right decode (Side inverted) 
 This three-track layout lets you adjust stereo width in real time by changing the level of MS L and MS R relative to MS C. It is a common approach in classical music post-production.
 Quick Verification
 After setting up the matrix, run these checks before moving on to the next task:
 Solo MS C and listen. You should hear a clear, stable center image with no stereo spread. If it sounds wide, the routing is incorrect. 
 Sum MS L and MS R together (both soloed). If the Side signal is correctly inverted, the Side components cancel and you are left with only the Mid signal, the same as MS C alone. 
 Confirm the EQ 3 polarity invert button is lit (active) on MS R only. If it is active on MS L or MS C by mistake, your decode will be wrong. 
 Volume Levels for the MS Tracks
 After decoding, set these fader levels on your three MS tracks:
 MS Track Fader Levels
 Track
 Fader Level
 02 - MS L
 -5.0 dB
 03 - MS C
 -5.0 dB
 04 - MS R
 -5.0 dB
 These three tracks are placed in the MS group and routed to the MS VCA (set to +3.0 dB), so the group controls all three simultaneously after individual levels are set.
 Tip: Set the individual fader levels on tracks 02, 03, and 04 before creating the group. Once they are in a group, moving any one fader moves all of them together. If you need to adjust a single track inside an active Mix Group, hold Control (Mac) while dragging the fader to clutch it out of the group temporarily. VCAs and routing folders avoid this problem entirely for the overall level, which is exactly why this assignment uses both.

pages.title: Calibration and Monitoring: Procedure Guide
pages.text:
Calibration and Monitoring: Procedure Guide 
 Calibration and Monitoring: Procedure Guide
 Follow this in order. Each step assumes the one before it is complete. If a step will not work, the cause is almost always something skipped earlier, not the step you are on.
 Figure 1. The Metering preferences. The Calibration Reference Level field at the lower left is what ties what you see on the meter to what you set in the room.
 Use this self-contained guide before completing the assignment work in this module. It explains the operating workflow; the corresponding assignment provides the required project-specific settings and submission evidence.
 Step-by-Step Workflow
 Open the supplied reference-noise file and route it through the same output path used for mixing.
 Set your monitoring controller to a repeatable reference position before changing monitor or interface gain.
 Measure the playback level at the listening position, make one controlled adjustment, then measure again. Record the final monitor position and level in the required document.
 Before submission, confirm that your written assessment distinguishes room observations from monitor-level settings.
 Reference: Apply the current Avid Pro Tools Reference Guide procedures that correspond to the tools used here. Keep an untouched playlist or session version before making destructive edits. 
 This page is self-contained and does not rely on links to other Canvas pages.
 Save before and after. Save the session before you start and again when you finish, with a version number in the name. It costs two seconds and it is the only undo that survives a crash.
 Figure 2. Every stage between the fader and the speaker has its own gain. Calibration is deciding which one of these you are allowed to move afterwards.

pages.title: "A Horse Is Not a Home"
pages.text:
Tuning: A Horse Is Not a Home, the Semester Project 
 Throughout the semester we will work on A_Horse_is_Not_a_Home-Consolidated.zip and develop it into a clean, organized, mix-ready and delivery-ready project. This lab is designed to reflect real industry workflow from session preparation through final mix and delivery.
 Tuning: A Horse Is Not a Home, the Semester Project
 Figure 1. Correction Speed Scoop.
 Develop a professional tempo map and session structure.
 Organize and route a complex session using industry standards.
 Apply pitch correction, editing, and mixing tools at a professional level.
 Create a mix that can be recalled, revised, delivered, and archived properly.
 Follow current professional delivery recommendations used by producers and engineers.
 Core Session File
 We will work from the session: A Horse is Not a Home – Consolidated .
 This session will be used throughout the semester for editing, organization, mixing, routing, and final delivery preparation.
 Tempo Mapping and Editing
 You will refine and correct the existing tempo map.
 You will create a clear, stable tempo map covering at least 24 bars .
 You will use class techniques including:
 Tempo ruler mapping and markers
 Elastic Audio
 Beat Detective
 Manual editing where appropriate
 Tempo and timing decisions must support musical feel, not just visual alignment.
 Pitch Correction and Editing
 We will apply professional pitch correction and editing workflows as part of the mix process.
 Apply pitch correction transparently and musically.
 Maintain natural timing and tone when correcting vocals and instruments.
 Commit or clearly label corrected tracks when appropriate.
 Ensure edited and tuned tracks remain organized and recallable.
 Mix Processing and Effects
 You will build a complete mix using professional signal flow and processing.
 Compression for tone control, dynamic shaping, and bus processing.
 Gates and expanders for cleanup and tone shaping.
 Equalization (EQ) for clarity, balance, and tone.
 Delay and reverb for space and depth.
 Additional creative effects as appropriate to the mix.
 All processing must be intentional, labeled, and recallable.
 Routing, VCAs, and Mix Structure
 Use both MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) and Instrument tracks appropriately.
 Create at least three VCA masters mapped to meaningful mix groups.
 Use routing folders or bus groups to keep the session organized.
 Maintain clear signal flow from source to master output.
 Create and maintain a clearly labeled master fader.
 Set up sidechain compression routing where appropriate.
 Create an internal layback track to print final mixes inside the session.
 Immersive and Multichannel Content
 This project includes 9.1 surround and Ambisonic material.
 Organize immersive tracks clearly.
 Mute, subgroup, or route immersive content intentionally.
 Avoid accidental routing to stereo or incorrect outputs.
 Maintain clear naming and color coding for immersive paths.
 Professional Session Organization
 Use clear and consistent track naming.
 Color code tracks by function or section.
 Remove unused tracks, plugins, and routing.
 Keep layout consistent and easy to navigate.
 Use comments and markers where helpful.
 Reference: Professional Delivery Guidelines
 We will follow current professional delivery and archival recommendations from:
 Delivery Recommendations for Recorded Music Projects (2025) 
Producers & Engineers Wing, The Recording Academy
 View Reference Document 
 These guidelines represent widely accepted industry standards for organizing, delivering, and archiving music projects.
 Key Professional Practices We Will Follow
 Session and File Organization
 All tracks should be consolidated and aligned with the same start and end time.
 All virtual instruments should be committed or documented when delivering sessions.
 File and session naming must be clear and consistent.
 Sessions must be organized so another engineer can open and understand them.
 Mix and Stem Preparation
 Print final approved mixes and alternate versions when required.
 Create organized stem sets that sum correctly to the mix.
 Ensure stems are consolidated and time aligned.
 Verify routing and processing before printing.
 Metadata and Documentation
 Maintain accurate session and project metadata.
 Include documentation for routing, processing, and mix decisions.
 Use clear folder hierarchy and labeling.
 Archiving and Backup
 Create multiple backups of final work.
 Maintain organized project folders.
 Preserve original recordings and mix sessions.
 Ensure projects can be reopened and recreated in the future.
 Professional engineers are responsible for ensuring recordings remain organized, accessible, and ready for future use or archival preservation.
 Evaluation Criteria
 Tempo map accuracy and editing quality.
 Pitch correction quality and transparency.
 Use of compression, EQ, gates, delay, and reverb.
 Session organization and routing clarity.
 Professional mix quality and documentation.
 Delivery readiness and adherence to guidelines.
 Professional Mindset
 A clean, organized session saves hours later and allows mixes to be revised, delivered, and archived without confusion. Remember that another engineer should be able to open your session and immediately understand your work.

Frequency Dynamics and Side-Chains: Procedure Guide 
 Frequency Dynamics and Side-Chains: Procedure Guide
 Follow this in order. Each step assumes the one before it is complete. If a step will not work, the cause is almost always something skipped earlier, not the step you are on.
 Figure 1. Pro Compressor with its Side-Chain section open. The Source menu is set to an external bus, which is how one track ends up controlling the compression on another.
 Use this self-contained guide before completing the assignment work in this module. It explains the operating workflow; the corresponding assignment provides the required project-specific settings and submission evidence.
 The Signal Path, Before You Touch a Control
 A side-chain is two signal paths, not one. The trigger track does the pushing. A key send carries a copy of it to the side chain input on the compressor, and the compressor, inserted on the ducked track, turns that key signal into gain reduction. You never hear the trigger through the compressor; you hear the ducked track dip each time the trigger hits. Read the diagram in number order before you open a single menu.
 Figure 2. The trigger track (1) feeds a key send (2) into the side chain input (3). The compressor (4) sits on the ducked track, and its output (5) dips each time the trigger hits.
 The five numbered points in the diagram, in signal order
 1
 Trigger track (the kick or voice that does the pushing)
 2
 Key send off the trigger track
 3
 Side chain (key) input on the compressor
 4
 The compressor, inserted on the ducked track
 5
 The compressor's output: its gain reduction pulls the ducked track down each time the trigger hits
 In Pro Compressor, point 3 is the Source menu in the Side-Chain section, shown in the screenshot at the top of this page. Set it to the bus the key send feeds, not to the ducked track's own signal.
 Step-by-Step Workflow
 Identify the masking relationship and decide which source should trigger control of the other source.
 Insert a dynamics processor on the controlled track, enable its key input, and route the trigger source to that key or side-chain bus.
 Filter the key signal when needed so only the frequency range causing the conflict drives gain reduction.
 Adjust threshold, ratio, attack, and release while listening to the full mix. Confirm that gain reduction occurs only when the trigger is present.

pages.title: Frequency Dynamics and Side-Chains: How They Work
pages.text:
Frequency Dynamics and Side-Chains: How They Work 
 Frequency Dynamics and Side-Chains: How They Work
 A side-chain is a compressor listening to something else. The audio you hear and the audio that triggers the gain reduction do not have to be the same signal. That one idea covers ducking, de-essing and frequency selective control.
 Figure 1. Pro Compressor with its Side-Chain section open. The Source menu is set to an external bus, which is how one track ends up controlling the compression on another.
 These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to.
 Each control and what it does
 Control
 What it does
 Key input 
 The signal that triggers the compressor, which is not the signal being compressed.
 Side-chain filter 
 Makes the compressor listen to only part of the spectrum. A high-pass here stops the kick pumping the whole mix.
 Multiband compression 
 Different compression per frequency band. Solves what static EQ cannot, and causes what static EQ never would.
 De-esser 
 A compressor keyed to the sibilant range. The same idea, one band, one job.
 Ducking 
 Using one source to pull another down. Voice over music is the obvious case, kick over bass is the useful one.
 Filter the key input first. Before you set threshold, high-pass the key input so the compressor stops reacting to low end you never wanted it to react to. Most of the time that alone fixes the pumping.
 Kick-triggered bass ducking is easy to overdo. Aim for 2 to 3 dB of reduction with a release that recovers before the next kick. If you can hear the bass breathe as a separate event, it is too much.
 Figure 2. The kick never passes through the compressor. It only tells the compressor when to pull the bass down, which is why the two stop fighting.

pages.text:
Master-Buss Processing and Endgame: Knowing When to Stop 
 Master-Buss Processing and Endgame: Knowing When to Stop
 The master buss is not where a mix gets fixed. If the mix needs 4 dB of master buss EQ, the problem is on a channel. Go back and find it. Master buss processing is for the last few percent, after the mix already works.
 Figure 1. Channel Strip, showing the EQ curve and the dynamics graph in one window. On a master buss every move here should be small enough to argue for.
 These are the controls this module turns on. Know what each one does before you decide what to set it to.
 Each control and what it does
 Control
 What it does
 Master fader 
 Post everything. Leave it at unity and control level upstream.
 Buss compression 
 Small amounts. 1 to 2 dB of gain reduction on the mix buss is a lot.
 Buss EQ 
 Broad moves only. If you need a narrow cut on the master, it belongs on a track.
 Limiting 
 For control, not for loudness, at this stage. Mastering is a different job with different ears.
 Headroom on delivery 
 Leave the peaks under 0 dBFS. What you deliver is not what a streaming service will play back.
 Leave headroom on delivery. Print with peaks around -6 dBFS and no limiter on the master unless the assignment asks for one. Mastering needs room to work, and a mix squashed flat gives it none.
 How to know you are done. You are done when your next three moves are all under 1 dB and you cannot say which one helped. Bounce it, leave it a day, and listen once in the car. If you still want to change something, it will be obvious in the first ten seconds.

 Every one of these is a mistake that gets made in this room every semester. The middle column is the part worth memorizing: what the mistake sounds like is how you catch it in your own work.
 Each mistake, the sound that gives it away, and what to do instead
 The mistake
 What you hear
 What to do instead
 Mix buss processing added at the end 
 Every balance decision was made without it, and adding it undoes them.
 Put it on early and mix into it, or leave it off.
 Chasing loudness on the master 
 The mix is loud, flat and tiring, and streaming will turn it down anyway.
 Mix for dynamics. Loudness normalization means the loud mix wins nothing.
 Not knowing when it is done 
 Endless revisions, each one different and none better.
 Leave it overnight. If you cannot name what is wrong the next morning, it is finished.
 Hearing it is the skill. Each mistake has a listening cue attached. Learn the cue and you stop needing the checklist.

pages.title: Distortion: What Is Actually Happening
pages.text:
Distortion: What Is Actually Happening 
 Distortion: What Is Actually Happening
 Distortion is a change in the shape of the waveform. Every distortion box, plugin and pedal does the same basic job: it bends the wave. Once you understand what that bending adds, you can predict what any distortion will do before you insert it.
 Clipping and waveshaping
 Every amplifier, converter and plugin can only swing so far. When the input asks for more than the circuit can deliver, the tops of the wave get squashed or cut off. That is clipping. Waveshaping is the general name for any process that maps each input value to a new output value through a curve, called a transfer curve. A clipper is simply a waveshaper whose curve bends over at the top and the bottom.
 Here is the key fact. A pure sine wave contains one frequency. Change its shape at all and you create new frequencies. When the same change happens on every cycle, the new frequencies land at whole number multiples of the original. Those are harmonics. A 100 Hz sine that gets clipped comes out with new energy at 200 Hz, 300 Hz, 400 Hz and up. On a single note, distortion adds harmonics above the fundamental, never below it.
 Figure 1. The same sine wave clean, soft clipped and hard clipped. Soft clipping rounds the peaks as they approach the ceiling. Hard clipping follows the wave exactly until the ceiling, then cuts it flat.
 Soft clipping versus hard clipping
 Soft clipping bends the peaks gradually. Small signals pass almost untouched, and the curve flattens more as the level climbs. Hard clipping is a straight line right up to a ceiling and then a flat wall. The difference you hear is how far up the spectrum the new harmonics reach.
 Soft clipping adds harmonics that fall away quickly, so most of the new energy sits in the low order harmonics close to the fundamental. It sounds thicker and warmer rather than obviously distorted. Hard clipping cuts sharp corners into the wave, and a sharp corner can only be drawn with strong high harmonics. The added energy reaches far up the spectrum, so hard clipping sounds brighter, buzzier and harsher.
 Figure 2. Harmonics measured from a clipped sine. Hard clipping keeps its upper harmonics much stronger: here the 11th harmonic is about 1.3 percent of the fundamental with hard clipping and under 0.2 percent with soft clipping. Only the asymmetric curve produces even harmonics.
 Even and odd harmonics
 Which harmonics appear depends on symmetry. If a circuit clips the top and the bottom of the wave the same way, it produces only odd harmonics: the 3rd, 5th, 7th and so on. If it treats the top and bottom differently, for example a single tube stage that runs out of room sooner on one side, it adds even harmonics as well: the 2nd, 4th, 6th and so on.
 The 2nd harmonic is one octave above the fundamental and the 4th is two octaves above, so even harmonics blend into the note and tend to sound warm, full and musical. The 3rd harmonic is an octave and a fifth up, still consonant, but the 5th, 7th and higher odd harmonics sit further from the notes of the scale, so strong odd order content tends to sound edgy, aggressive or harsh. Treat this as a tendency, not a law. A little 3rd harmonic from tape or a transformer sounds great, and heavy even order distortion can still sound nasty. How far up the harmonics reach matters as much as whether they are even or odd.
 Clipping shape, the harmonics it adds, and how it tends to sound
 Clipping shape
 Harmonics added
 Typical sound
 Soft, symmetric
 Odd harmonics that fall away quickly
 Smooth thickening with a gentle edge
 Hard, symmetric
 Odd harmonics that stay strong far up the spectrum
 Bright, buzzy, aggressive
 Asymmetric
 Even and odd harmonics
 Warm, full, rounder
 Input level and gain staging drive it
 A distortion stage does not care what its knob is called. What matters is how hard the signal hits the curve. Turn up the input, or feed it a hotter track, and more of each cycle lands on the bent part of the curve, so more harmonics come out. Turn the input down and the same plugin gets cleaner. That means every level change upstream changes the character of every nonlinear stage downstream. If you raise a vocal 6 dB with clip gain before a saturation plugin, you did not just make it louder, you made it more distorted.
 This is why distortion plugins have separate drive and output controls. Drive sets how much the signal distorts. Output only sets how loud the result is. After you set the drive, use the output control to bring the level back to where it was, so you judge the tone and not the volume.
 Louder fools you. Added harmonics increase perceived loudness without raising peak level. Clipping also flattens the peaks, so a distorted signal can read the same or lower on a peak meter and still sound louder. Match loudness before you decide the distorted version is better.
 Intermodulation distortion: chords versus single notes
 Feed a single note into a distortion and every new frequency is a harmonic of that note, so it still sounds like one note, only thicker. Feed it two or more notes at once and the circuit also creates sum and difference frequencies between them. This is intermodulation distortion. Play 200 Hz and 300 Hz together through a clipper and you also get 100 Hz, 500 Hz and a web of other products.
 With simple intervals those products line up with the notes. A root and a fifth have a 3:2 ratio, so their difference tone lands an octave below the root, which is why power chords survive heavy gain and even sound bigger. A full major or minor chord contains thirds that do not line up so neatly, especially in equal temperament, so the intermodulation products land between the notes and the chord turns into mud and beating. When a heavily distorted chord sounds like mush, the fix is fewer notes or less gain, not more EQ.
 Test with a single note, then a chord. If a single note sounds great and a full chord sounds muddy, you are hearing intermodulation. Back off the drive or simplify the voicing before you reach for an EQ.

pages.title: Distortion: Digital Clipping, Analog Saturation and Blown Speakers
pages.text:
Distortion: Digital Clipping, Analog Saturation and Blown Speakers 
 Distortion: Digital Clipping, Analog Saturation and Blown Speakers
 Every system has a ceiling. What changes from one system to the next is what happens when you hit it. Digital stops dead, analog bends, and speakers break. Each one leaves a sound you should be able to recognize.
 Digital clipping at 0 dBFS
 A digital system stores each sample as a number, and full scale is the largest number it can store. That ceiling is 0 dBFS, decibels relative to full scale. In a fixed point file or at the converter nothing can go above it. When the signal asks for more, every sample that would have gone over is stored as full scale instead, so the top of the wave is cut perfectly flat. This is the hardest clipping there is: a straight line and then a wall, with no bend at all.
 Most DAWs mix internally in floating point, so a channel meter that touches red does not always mean that channel has clipped. The damage happens where the signal becomes fixed point again: the output converter, a 24 bit bounce, or a plugin that clips internally. Do not lean on that. Keep channels and the master out of the red, because anything that reaches the converter or a bounced file above 0 dBFS will clip.
 Figure 1. A digital over stores every sample above full scale as full scale, leaving flat tops with sharp corners. Analog saturation bends the same peaks gradually.
 Why digital overs sound harsh
 Two things make a digital over sound worse than an analog one. First, the flat top with sharp corners creates strong high harmonics, like any hard clipper. Second, those harmonics do not stop at the top of the audio band. A digital system can only represent frequencies up to half its sample rate, the Nyquist frequency, which is 22.05 kHz at a 44.1 kHz sample rate. Harmonics generated above that point do not disappear. They fold back down into the audible range at frequencies that have no musical relationship to the note. This is aliasing, and it sounds like a gritty, metallic, inharmonic edge rather than a thicker version of the note.
 Figure 2. A 2.5 kHz sine hard clipped with no oversampling. The green lines are true harmonics. The orange lines are aliases folded back from above Nyquist, including one at 700 Hz, far below the note that caused it.
 Well designed distortion plugins reduce aliasing by oversampling. They run the distortion at two, four or more times the session sample rate, filter out everything above the audio band, and then return to the session rate. If a saturation plugin sounds grainy or metallic on high notes, look for an oversampling setting and raise it.
 How analog rounds off
 Analog circuits cannot jump from a straight line to a wall. Tubes, tape and transformers run out of room gradually, so they soft clip, and many transistor circuits start soft as well. Analog stages also create harmonics above 20 kHz, but there is no sample rate for those to fold back against, so they simply fall away above hearing. Each device has its own curve.
 How common analog stages saturate
 Device
 How it saturates
 Typical character
 Tubes
 A soft curve; a single ended stage clips one side sooner than the other
 Strong 2nd harmonic, warm and thick
 Tape
 Magnetic saturation rounds and compresses the peaks; highs soften when driven hard
 Smooth, mostly 3rd harmonic, transients glued together
 Transformers
 The core saturates, most of all on low frequencies
 Weight and a little grit in the lows
 Transistors
 Soft at first, and they can clip hard when pushed
 Warm to edgy depending on the circuit
 Op amps
 Clean right up to the supply rail, then a hard clip
 Harsh and buzzy, close to a digital over
 Inter sample peaks and true peak
 A sample peak meter only reads the stored samples. The converter does not play samples; it draws a smooth waveform through them. That waveform can swing higher than any stored sample, especially after heavy limiting or clipping. These are inter sample peaks. A file whose highest sample reads exactly 0 dBFS can reconstruct to a peak above full scale and clip the converter or the encoder on a streaming service.
 Figure 3. Every stored sample sits at or below 0 dBFS, but the waveform the converter rebuilds between them peaks about 3 dB higher. A sample peak meter never sees it; a true peak meter does.
 A true peak meter oversamples the signal to estimate the reconstructed peak and reports it in dBTP. Many streaming delivery specifications ask for true peaks no higher than minus 1 dBTP. A mix going to mastering needs far more room than that: print with peaks around minus 6 dBFS, as the Knowing When to Stop page says.
 What a blown speaker sounds like
 Speakers distort too, and a damaged speaker has a sound you should learn to recognize so you do not blame your mix for it. A speaker is a paper or plastic cone driven by a voice coil that moves in a narrow magnetic gap. Three common failures:
 Torn cone or loose surround. The torn edges flap and slap against each other, adding a buzz or rattle that rides on top of the loud notes.
 Voice coil rub. Heat or a hard knock deforms the coil or knocks it off center, so it scrapes the magnet as it moves. It sounds like a scratchy, papery distortion.
 Bottoming out. The cone is asked to move further than its suspension allows and hits its mechanical limit, which sounds like a hard crackle on loud bass notes.
 All three are mechanical, so they are worst when the cone moves the most, and the cone moves the most on loud, low notes. To check, pan the offending part to the other side. If the buzz moves with the part, it is in the mix. If the buzz stays in the same physical speaker, the speaker is damaged.
 A short history: cutting the cone on purpose
 Before distortion pedals were common, players who wanted a buzzing, fuzzy tone got it by damaging their gear. In the late 1950s and early 1960s guitarists poked holes in speaker cones with pencils, slit them with razor blades, and pushed knitting needles through them. Link Wray punched holes in his amplifier speaker with a pencil, and Dave Davies of the Kinks slit the speaker cone of a small amplifier with a razor blade for the band's raw early sound. The torn paper rattled on every note, adding exactly the buzz described above. Around the same time a faulty channel on a studio console produced a fuzzy bass tone on a 1961 Nashville session, and that sound helped lead to the first commercial fuzz pedals: a way to get a broken speaker's sound without breaking anything.
 Do not damage monitors to find out what this sounds like. Keep studio monitor levels sane, turn monitors on last and off first, and listen for rattle and rub on low, loud material. A monitor that buzzes will mislead every decision you make about distortion.

pages.title: Distortion: Overdrive, Distortion, Fuzz, Buzz and Other Pedals
pages.text:
Distortion: Overdrive, Distortion, Fuzz, Buzz and Other Pedals 
 Distortion: Overdrive, Distortion, Fuzz, Buzz and Other Pedals
 The name on the box describes how hard the circuit clips. Brand names come and go. The categories below describe circuits, and once you know the circuit you can predict the sound of any pedal or plugin that copies it.
 The clearest way to compare these circuits is the transfer curve: input level across the bottom, output level up the side. A clean stage is a straight diagonal line. Every kind of distortion bends that line somewhere.
 Figure 1. Transfer curves. Overdrive bends gradually, distortion runs straight into a hard ceiling, and fuzz has so much gain that almost any input jumps straight to the ceiling, turning notes into near square waves.
 Overdrive
 An overdrive is a soft clipper built to behave like a tube amplifier pushed a little past clean. The classic circuit puts clipping diodes in the feedback loop of an op amp, so the diodes round the peaks more as the gain rises, and some clean signal always blends with the clipped signal. The result is mostly low order harmonics, gentle compression, and a tone that follows your picking: play softly and it cleans up, dig in and it breaks up. Many overdrives also trim lows before the clipping and add a midrange hump, which keeps the low end tight. Reach for overdrive when a part should sound pushed and alive rather than obviously distorted, or to push an amplifier that is already on the edge.
 Distortion
 A distortion circuit uses more gain and clips hard, usually with diodes to ground after a high gain stage, so the peaks hit a fixed ceiling and flatten. You get stronger harmonics reaching higher up, heavy compression, long sustain, and far less response to picking dynamics. It sounds thick, aggressive and consistent from note to note. Reach for it for heavy rhythm parts, leads that need to sustain, and parts that should hold one intensity.
 Fuzz and buzz
 A fuzz is the oldest and simplest design: two or three transistors with a lot of gain and very little else. It drives the signal so far into clipping that a sustained note becomes nearly a square wave, which is rich in strong odd harmonics. Fuzz sounds woolly, buzzy and huge. It also reacts to the guitar volume knob: roll the guitar volume back and many fuzz circuits clean up surprisingly well.
 Starve a fuzz of voltage or bias its transistors off center and the character changes. The transistor only passes signal when the input is strong, so as a note decays it drops below that threshold and the output breaks into a sputtering, gated buzz before cutting off completely. Players call this a gated or velcro fuzz. It is the most broken sounding pedal on the board, and that is why people use it: it recreates the torn speaker sound from the previous page on purpose. Some fuzz circuits also rectify the signal, flipping the bottom half of the wave upward. That doubles the frequency and adds an octave up effect on top of the fuzz.
 Bitcrushers and decimators
 Bitcrushers and decimators distort digitally, in a completely different way. A bitcrusher reduces bit depth: it forces each sample onto a coarser set of levels, so a smooth wave becomes a staircase. The error between the real wave and the staircase is quantization distortion, which sounds like grainy, gritty noise that follows the signal and gets worse as the signal gets quieter.
 A decimator reduces the sample rate by holding each sample for several sample periods. That lowers the Nyquist frequency, so anything above the new limit folds back as aliasing: metallic, inharmonic tones that do not follow the pitch. It is the sound of early samplers and old video game consoles.
 Figure 2. Left, bit depth reduction forces the wave onto eight levels. Right, sample rate reduction holds each value for a long stretch. Both turn a smooth sine into steps, but they add different kinds of distortion.
 Reach for these when a sound should feel lo fi, digital or synthetic: a drum loop, a vocal hook in a breakdown, a synth that needs grit. They are poor choices when you want warmth, because what they add is stepped, jagged detail and aliasing rather than smooth low order harmonics.
 Amp and tape saturation plugins
 Amp simulators model a whole chain: several gain stages that each soft clip a little, a tone stack, a power amp that compresses, and then a speaker cabinet. The cabinet matters as much as the gain. A guitar speaker rolls off steeply above roughly 5 kHz, which removes the fizzy top that raw clipping produces. That is why a distortion pedal plugged straight into a console sounds thin and fizzy, while the same pedal into an amp or a cabinet simulation sounds like a guitar.
 Tape saturation plugins model magnetic tape driven hard: soft clipping that is mostly 3rd harmonic, gentle compression, and a slight softening of the top end at high levels. Tape saturation softens and rounds transients, lowering peak level while keeping apparent loudness, which is why it is popular on drums, bass and the mix buss.
 Distortion types compared
 Type
 How it clips
 What it sounds like
 Reach for it when
 Overdrive
 Soft, diodes in the feedback loop
 Warm, dynamic, low order harmonics
 A part should sound pushed but natural
 Distortion
 Hard, diodes to ground after high gain
 Thick, compressed, bright
 Heavy rhythm parts and sustaining leads
 Fuzz
 Nearly square wave from very high gain

 A part should sound huge, vintage or broken
 Gated fuzz
 Starved transistor cuts off as notes decay
 Sputtering and splatty
 You want a deliberately failing sound
 Bitcrusher
 Bit depth reduction, stepped levels

 Lo fi or digital textures
 Decimator

 Metallic and inharmonic
 Synthetic or retro game textures

 Amp simulator

 A guitar amp in a room

 Choose by the job, not the name. Ask what the part needs. A little more weight and life calls for overdrive or tape. Constant aggression calls for distortion. Something huge or broken calls for fuzz. Something digital calls for a bitcrusher or decimator.

pages.title: Distortion: Guitars, Pickups and Using Distortion in a Mix
pages.text:
Distortion: Guitars, Pickups and Using Distortion in a Mix 
 Distortion: Guitars, Pickups and Using Distortion in a Mix
 Distortion works on what you feed it. The same pedal or plugin sounds completely different depending on the pickup, the level, and the EQ in front of it. Control those and you control the distortion.
 Bridge and neck pickups
 A vibrating string moves in many modes at once: the whole string swinging (the fundamental), the string in halves (the 2nd harmonic), in thirds, and so on. Both ends of the string are fixed, so nothing moves at the ends. Close to a fixed end every mode moves only a little, but the upper modes, which vibrate in short segments, move a lot compared with the fundamental. The bridge pickup sits near that fixed end, so it hears a signal where the upper partials are strong relative to the fundamental: brighter, thinner, with more bite. The neck pickup sits further toward the middle of the string, where the fundamental swings widely, so it hears more fundamental and relatively less upper harmonic content: warmer and rounder. It also sits close to points where some harmonics barely move, which notches those harmonics out.
 Figure 1. Illustrative only, from an idealized string model with the same pluck. Each pickup is scaled to its own fundamental. The bridge pickup keeps its upper harmonics strong; the neck pickup falls away and even loses the 4th and 8th harmonics.
 This matters twice once distortion is involved. First, distortion creates new harmonics from the harmonics it is fed. A bridge pickup gives the distortion more high frequency content to work with, so the result is bright and articulate and cuts through a dense mix. A neck pickup through the same distortion sounds thicker and smoother, but it can disappear behind cymbals, keys and vocals. Second, the neck pickup puts more of its energy in the lows, which drives the distortion harder down there, so heavy gain on the neck pickup turns muddy sooner.
 Gain is not volume
 On an amp or a pedal, gain (or drive) sets how hard the signal hits the clipping stage. Volume (or level, or master) sets how loud the result is after the clipping. High gain at low volume is still a heavily distorted sound, just quiet. Low gain at high volume is a clean sound, just loud. When a guitar part needs to be bigger, more gain is usually the wrong answer; more level, a better pickup choice, or a double tracked part usually works better.
 Distortion compresses and adds sustain
 Clipping is a kind of instant limiting. Once the signal hits the ceiling, playing harder barely makes it louder, and as a note decays the gain holds it up near the ceiling until it finally falls below the clipping point. So distortion reduces the dynamic range of a part and adds sustain, and more gain means more of both. That is why a heavily distorted guitar rarely needs a compressor, and why a clean part that needs sustain can often get it from a little overdrive instead.
 When there is too much gain
 Past a point, more gain costs you. Each note carries so many harmonics and intermodulation products that chords blur, picking detail disappears, and single notes lose definition. The low end suffers first. Low strings make the biggest swings and drive the circuit hardest, and their harmonics and difference tones pile up in the low mids, so the bottom gets flubby and loose instead of tight.
 Figure 2. A gain chain that keeps the low end tight. Filter the lows before the drive, shape the tone after it, and set the level last.
 The fix is EQ on both sides of the drive. Put a high pass filter before the drive, somewhere around 80 to 150 Hz on a guitar, so the distortion never sees the low content that turns to mud. Then shape the tone after the drive, taming fizz up top and harshness in the upper mids. On bass, put corrective EQ before the distortion so you are distorting the tone you actually want.
 Saturation as a mix tool
 Parallel saturation on drums. Send the drums to an aux with heavy saturation and blend it under the dry kit. The dry signal keeps its transients and dynamics while the distorted signal adds weight and density. On a drum buss that already sounds lifeless from compression, a parallel saturation blend adds harmonic content and apparent loudness without squashing the dry transients any further.
 Parallel saturation on vocals. Blend a saturated copy under the lead vocal to help it read on small speakers and through a busy chorus, with a high pass on the saturated copy so it adds presence and not mud.
 Saturation on bass. Phone and laptop speakers cannot reproduce the fundamental of a low bass note. Saturation adds harmonics above the fundamental that imply the pitch the speaker cannot produce, and the ear fills in the missing fundamental.
 Cutting through without more level. A distorted guitar that sounds great alone can vanish in the mix because its harmonics fill the midrange where vocals, keys and snare also live. Try a brighter pickup, less gain, or a post EQ cut in the competing parts before you push the fader.
 Listen to the consonants. When saturation on a vocal goes too far, sibilance turns harsh and the consonants become brittle. Back off the drive, or high pass and de ess the saturated copy.
 Check distortion at matched loudness
 Distortion raises perceived loudness, and ears almost always prefer the louder version. Before you decide a saturated track is better, use the plugin output control to match the loudness of the processed and dry versions, then switch between them. If you still prefer it at the same loudness, keep it. Then check once more on small speakers, where saturation often makes its biggest difference.
 A quick routine. Choose the pickup, high pass before the drive, set the drive by ear, shape the tone after it, match the loudness, then decide.
